A_target.statement:
Let ${}^* \R$ be a [[Definition:Hyperreal Number|hyperreal]] extension of $\R$ and $f: \R \to \R$ [[Definition:Differentiable Real Function|differentiable]] at $x$.
Then for every non-zero [[Definition:Infinitesimal|infinitesimal]] $\d x$:
:$\map {f'} x = \map {\operatorname {st} } {\dfrac {\map {{}^* f} {x + \d x} - \map f x} {\d x} }$
where $\operatorname {st}$ is the [[Definition:Standard Part|standard part]].

B_source.statement:
Let $f: \R \to \R$.
Then $f$ is [[Definition:Differentiable Real Function|differentiable]] at $x$ with derivative $L$ {{iff}}:
:$\forall \epsilon > 0: \exists \delta > 0: 0 < \size h < \delta \implies \size {\dfrac {\map f {x + h} - \map f x} h - L} < \epsilon$

substitutions.the real line: a nonstandard extension containing infinitesimals and unlimited numbers
substitutions.the limit of the difference quotient: the standard part of the difference quotient

derived.first-order statements about the reals: transferred verbatim by the transfer principle
derived.statements quantifying over subsets: not transferred automatically, since they are not first order

object_map.reformulation: Move to an extended number system where limiting conditions become algebraic conditions on infinitesimals.

validity_conditions: The transfer principle guarantees that a first-order statement holds in the reals exactly when it holds in the nonstandard extension, which is what licenses the whole translation.
The standard part function is defined only on limited elements, so each use must check the quantity is not unlimited.
Second-order statements do not transfer: the least upper bound property fails for internal sets in the naive form, so completeness arguments must be reformulated rather than copied.
proof_plan: Pass to a nonstandard extension ${}^* \R \supseteq \R$ containing non-zero [[Definition:Infinitesimal|infinitesimals]].
Restate the $\epsilon$-$\delta$ definition: $L$ is the derivative {{iff}} the difference quotient is [[Definition:Infinitely Close|infinitely close]] to $L$ for every non-zero infinitesimal $h$.
By the [[Transfer Principle]], first-order statements about $f$ hold in $\R$ {{iff}} they hold for ${}^* f$ in ${}^* \R$.
